questions.q: What are the four pieces that go into the research portfolio, per this lesson?
options: Four separate GitHub accounts, one per project
The Project 1, 2, and 3 write-ups plus the interpretability finding
Three write-ups and a resume
A single combined notebook with no written summary
questions.explain: The portfolio assembles the three project write-ups (Lessons 9, 14, 20) and the interpretability finding (Lesson 24) into one artifact.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what kind of work does assembling the portfolio actually involve?
options: Running all three projects again from scratch
Assembly of already-finished artifacts into a consistent layout, not new research
Writing an entirely new fourth research project
Deleting the original write-ups and starting over
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that nothing new gets created — the work is pulling four already-finished pieces into one consistent shape.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the root README in the suggested repo layout?
options: To list every dependency version used across all three projects
To give a one-page summary of each project with its headline result, so nobody has to open a notebook to learn what you found
To replace the need for any of the individual write-ups
To store the raw training logs
questions.explain: The root README is the one-page summary of the whole portfolio — three or four sentences per project plus the headline number — so the story is clear before anyone opens a notebook.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say an honestly reported negative result can read as more credible than a suspiciously perfect win?
options: Because hiring managers always prefer failures over successes
Because negative results require less code to produce
Because a well-reported null result shows honest evidence-gathering, which a hiring manager scans for
Because positive results are against the portfolio's rules
questions.explain: The lesson frames evidence of a real result — even a negative one, reported honestly — as exactly what a hiring manager is scanning for, more so than a result that looks too good to be true.

questions.q: What does this lesson warn will undo everything a write-up claims?
options: Using Markdown instead of plain text for the write-up
A cloned repo that errors out on line one
Having more than one project in the same repo
Including a one-page summary alongside a notebook
questions.explain: Code that doesn't actually run — a clone that errors out immediately — undermines every claim made in the accompanying write-up.
